summary: States the problem and requirements for more accurate Explicit Congestion Notification feedback in TCP. Current ECN feedback can report only one congestion signal per round trip, which limits what congestion control can do. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A traffic light that says one car is stuck per minute even if ten are. This asks for a better report of how many cars were affected.

subtitle: What a better TCP congestion feedback signal would have to do, before anyone designs it.

tldr.problem: Classic ECN in TCP can report only one congestion signal per round-trip time, even when several packets were marked. Newer mechanisms such as DCTCP and ConEx need to know how many were marked.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC does not define a protocol. It lists use cases and seven requirements (resilience, timeliness, integrity, accuracy, complexity, overhead, compatibility) and sketches three design approaches to compare against them.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational problem statement that guides later protocol work. It also aims to stop each DCTCP implementation from inventing its own incompatible handshake.

today: RFC 7560 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It states requirements and does not define a protocol itself.

sections.title: Why Classic ECN Feedback Is Too Coarse
sections.content:
Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) lets network nodes mark IP packets instead of dropping them to signal congestion. The receiver feeds this back to the sender. In TCP, ECN is specified so that only one feedback signal can be sent per Round-Trip Time (RTT).

That is enough for classic TCP congestion control, which cuts its sending rate once per RTT no matter how many marks arrive. But Congestion Exposure (ConEx) and Data Center TCP (DCTCP) need to know about every marking in an RTT. DCTCP implementations already change TCP's ECN feedback in proprietary ways and skip capability negotiation. A main motivation of the RFC is to step in before each one invents its own non-interoperable handshake and uses up the few remaining flags and codepoints.

The requirements cover only the type and quality of the feedback signal. They do not say how a sender should react to it, and they do not make changes to senders or receivers obligatory.
sections.eli5: Today the receiver can only say 'there was congestion' once per round trip. Some newer programs want to know how many packets were hit, so this document asks for a better way to tell them.

sections.title: Recap of Classic ECN and the ECN Nonce
sections.content:
ECN uses two bits in the IP header, giving four codepoints: Not-ECT, ECT(0), ECT(1) and CE (Congestion Experienced). In the TCP header, the receiver signals a CE mark with the ECE flag and keeps setting it on every ACK. The sender sets the CWR flag once it has reacted. This always produces a full RTT of ACKs with ECE set, so extra CE marks in that RTT cannot be reported.

The ECN Nonce (RFC 3540) is an experimental addition that lets a sender detect concealed CE marks or drops. It adds the NS (Nonce Sum) flag. The RFC notes there are no known deployments of a TCP stack that uses it.

An alternative integrity check has been proposed in which the sender occasionally inserts a CE mark itself, or reorders packets, and checks that the receiver reports it faithfully. That would use no header bits and would free ECT(1) and the NS flag for other uses.
sections.eli5: The receiver waves a flag until the sender waves back, and that takes a whole round trip. Anything that happens while the flag is already up cannot be counted.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
ConEx is an experimental approach in which a sender relays the receiver's congestion feedback into the network along the forward path, so traffic can be managed by the congestion it causes rather than by rate or volume. ConEx already gets accurate loss feedback from selective acknowledgements, but TCP has had no equivalent for ECN.

DCTCP gives very low and predictable queuing delay. It needs ECN-enabled switches with a low step threshold and no signal smoothing, so it is currently used only in private networks such as data centers. Its own feedback protocol only works if there are no losses at all, and otherwise gets confused (Appendix A of the RFC). A generic accurate feedback scheme would remove the need for a consistent DCTCP variant network-wide and would cope with ACK loss.

Classic ECN TCP would neither benefit nor suffer. Senders could also use the more accurate feedback for integrity checks by randomly marking a few packets with CE themselves and checking that feedback arrives.
sections.eli5: Some systems, like a busy data center, need a precise count of problems, not just a yes or no. Ordinary senders do fine with yes or no and can ignore the extra detail.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
The feedback should be fairly accurate (not necessarily perfect), timely and protected. The RFC lists these requirements, which any proposal should discuss:

  • Resilience: feedback rides in ACKs, which can be lost, thinned or delayed, so it must still work under high congestion and with delayed ACKs.
  • Timeliness: feedback should arrive within about one RTT.
  • Integrity: at least as good as the ECN Nonce, or strong incentives for honest cooperation. The Nonce itself is not required, and the NS flag could be reused.
  • Accuracy: at least one notification per RTT as classic ECN gives, ideally the exact count of marks or marked bytes. Feeding back two of CE, ECT(1) and the sender's default is enough to infer the third. If feedback is sometimes lost, it should not be biased.
  • Complexity: as simple as possible, with minimal extra state.
  • Overhead: ideally no additional segments compared with RFC 3168 and minimal per-segment cost.
  • Backward and forward compatibility: negotiated between endpoints, with fallback to classic ECN and the aim to traverse middleboxes such as firewalls and NATs.

The ordering is not an order of importance, and candidates should justify any deviation.
sections.eli5: A good report must survive lost messages, arrive quickly, be hard to fake, be fairly exact, be simple, be small, and still work with older computers.

sections.title: Three Design Approaches
sections.content:
The RFC sketches approaches without endorsing any, to show the trade-offs.

Redefine the ECN/NS bits. A naive 1-bit scheme sends one ECE per CE mark. DCTCP's scheme toggles ECE on an immediate ACK whenever the CE marking changes, but it is ambiguous if pure ACKs are lost. Using ECE, CWR and NS together as a 3-bit counter of CE marks is more resilient, but the counter wraps often, so a short run of lost pure ACKs can lose information.

Use other header bits. There are three unused TCP flags that could extend the counter. Bits of the Urgent Pointer field could carry more counter bits when the Urgent flag is not set. Middleboxes might discard or normalize such bits, and assigning them would need an IETF standards action.

Use a TCP option. An option could carry as much detail as ECN for RTP over UDP or the SCTP proposal. To be resilient it would have to appear on most ACKs, adding considerable overhead, and new TCP options have deployment challenges of their own.
sections.eli5: You could change the meaning of flags already on the envelope, find unused space on it, or attach a separate note. Each choice costs something different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ECN feedback must only be used if the rest of the TCP segment shows it genuinely belongs to the flow and was not spoofed. Normal TCP acceptance checks apply, and feedback is only accepted on valid ACKs.

If feedback is lost and recovery is inadequate, congestion control will not react properly, which is why resilience is a requirement. ECN is not the last resort against congestion collapse: if the response to ECN is insufficient, loss follows and TCP reacts to loss. A receiver could also suppress feedback and make its connections use excess resources, as with classic ECN, which the integrity requirement is meant to address.
sections.eli5: Only believe a congestion report if it comes from the real conversation, and watch out for a receiver that hides bad news.
